Victims / Targets: Equinor (Norwegian state-majority energy company, Europe's largest gas supplier); certain IT systems, reportedly internal email
Summary: Equinor detected a cyberattack against certain IT systems on 17 Nov 2026 and worked with Norwegian national security authorities to neutralise it; Reuters (via The Record) reported internal email was down. Oil and gas production was not disrupted. On 20 Nov Equinor said "The cyber-attack against Equinor has now been stopped", with no sign that data was stolen or altered, and that it had been reported to the police. Equinor has not identified the attackers.
Notes: No IOCs or technical details published. Equinor's own statement was not read directly (quoted by Offshore Energy).

Incident: European Commission AI-assisted cyberattack disrupting internal services
Victims / Targets: European Commission; Sysper (HR), MyPMO (medical reimbursement) and translation systems taken down, most since restored
Summary: The European Commission confirmed that hackers attacked it in late October 2026 (detected 22 Oct, confirmed 26 Oct) and that an AI tool was used; several applications were taken down "as a protective and preventive measure" and most have been restored. Spokesperson Thomas Regnier did not attribute the attack to a known group, did not name the AI tool, said no data breach affecting staff had been found and knew of no ransom demand. Politico (via SecurityWeek) reported that attackers potentially compromised large amounts of data and disruption lasted over 10 days. SecurityWeek places it alongside CERT-EU's warning about ARTEX, but the Commission has not said ARTEX was the tool.
Notes: No IOCs published. Possible link to [[artex-2026]] is not confirmed by the Commission; CERT-EU's ARTEX blog and Politico's report were not read directly this run.

Incident: Qubole cross-account AWS access abused to breach customer cloud environments
Victims / Targets: Dozens of Qubole customers' AWS environments (Sentra); downstream exposure reported by J.P. Morgan Chase (marketing data: some customer names and email addresses), Mastercard (email addresses of a small subset of cardholders in one benefit program) and Visa (an Asia Pacific provider; Visa's systems not involved)
Actors (as reported): n0n (Wiz (11 Nov update, citing Risky Business): an actor calling themselves "n0n" claimed responsibility; Wiz: no ties to other public activity, targeting "opportunistic" and not typical of state-backed priorities. BleepingComputer: n0n ransomware group claimed the Qubole attack)
Summary: Wiz (with Sentra and Mandiant): between 14 and 26 Oct 2026 an actor used IAM credentials of two IAM users in the AWS account Qubole's platform uses (805246085872) to assume IAM roles customers had created to trust Qubole, then enumerated accounts, harvested secrets from Lambda, Secrets Manager and SSM, validated AWS, Entra ID and Okta credentials with TruffleHog and exfiltrated S3 data, mostly from an OVH VPS (57.129.54[.]120) and Mullvad VPN addresses. Sentra: dozens of victims, millions of files stolen from one customer, 100+ passwords and keys read within minutes. Wiz also saw a separate, unlinked Qubole-related set of activity (8-11 Oct) using customer-owned AWS access keys. AWS: its services were not compromised. On 16 Nov n0n leaked Chase, Visa and Mastercard data on its extortion site; on 20 Nov Chase said third-party service providers were attacked and marketing data accessed (BleepingComputer links this to Qubole; Qubole had not commented).
Reporters: Wiz; CSO Online (citing Sentra); BleepingComputer; BleepingComputer
Notes: IOCs transcribed from Wiz's four IOC tables. The TruffleHog user agent is omitted (also used by legitimate security teams). Sentra's own report was not read; its IOCs, if any, are not included. The link between Qubole and the Chase/Visa/Mastercard exposure is BleepingComputer's reporting of n0n's claim; Qubole/Idera had not confirmed it as of 2026-11-20.

Incident: ARTEX agentic AI penetration-testing framework abused in intrusions
Victims / Targets: Hundreds of organizations; South Korean banks (loan-inquiry and employee mobile systems); IT and software vendors and their downstream Microsoft 365 tenants via ConnectWise multi-tenant app credentials; exposed web APIs and identity providers
Sectors: Financial services; Cryptocurrency; Government; Telecommunications; Defense; Aerospace; Semiconductors; Technology; Software; Pharmaceuticals
Actors (as reported): Storm-0940 (Microsoft: China-state aligned actor); Vapor Panda (CrowdStrike (via Talos): China-nexus espionage campaign from 17 Oct 2026); Storm-3358 (Talos: financially motivated, Cambodia-based, targets financial organizations in Southeast Asia); Unnamed Chinese-speaking actor (CrowdStrike: likely Chinese-speaking and financially motivated (moderate confidence))
Summary: ARTEX, an open-source autonomous multi-agent AI penetration-testing framework published in July 2026 (closed-sourced on 8 Oct after 12,000+ forks), has been used by several unrelated actors; Talos says it is largely used by financially motivated criminals and China-nexus actors, so ARTEX use alone does not identify an actor. An LLM planner drives worker agents running nmap, nuclei, httpx, ffuf and curl. CrowdStrike: an unnamed, likely Chinese-speaking, financially motivated actor breached South Korean bank systems and exfiltrated data (late Sep to early Oct). Microsoft: China-state aligned Storm-0940 password-sprayed 2,250+ tenants (10-14 Oct) and abused ConnectWise multi-tenant application credentials for a supply-chain compromise, in some cases gaining privileged cloud access in under 3 hours; Wiz saw the same actor expand to other IT and software vendors. Unit 42: intrusion attempts (24 Sep-27 Oct) harvested JS source maps and OpenAPI specs, probed OAuth flows, self-registered accounts and read ~50 MB of API data; infrastructure serves WWW-Authenticate Basic realm="ARTEX" and a Sub2API LLM gateway. FBI FLASH-20261113-001 (TLP:CLEAR) gives network and behavioral IOCs, names no state sponsor, and lists Storm-3358 WISP C2 nodes and ARTEX servers (Microsoft). SentinelOne ties VAPOR PANDA's ARTEX use to BLOODALCHEMY malware. Separately, BadByte found trojanized ARTEX Docker images (tomicdd/artex, congdonglinux/artex; 7,946 pulls) whose /app/artex binary runs the login request's captcha field via sh -c as root before authentication, i.e. anyone running that image was exposed; Docker removed both images on 5 Nov 2026.
Reporters: Cisco Talos; Microsoft Threat Intelligence; CrowdStrike; Wiz; Palo Alto Networks Unit 42; FBI (FLASH-20261113-001); SentinelOne; BadByte; Kodem Security
Keywords: ARTEX; Sub2API; lanmao666; BLOODALCHEMY; Storm-0940; Storm-3358; Vapor Panda; tomicdd
Notes: Talos and Unit 42 note that not all ARTEX activity is malicious (it is also used for authorized testing), so these IPs are indicators to investigate rather than block outright. Generic user agents (curl, python-requests, Python-urllib) are omitted. SentinelOne's appendix also lists SHA-256 hashes for VAPOR PANDA's GameHook binary and BLOODALCHEMY loader/payload, an ARTEX TLS certificate hash and Hunt.io-sourced IPs; they were not added because the page could not be read verbatim past mid-appendix.
IOC Types: sha256 1, ipv4 2582, domain 6, user-agent 6, http-header 1, docker-image 3, app-id 3, other 2

Actors (as reported): TraderTraitor (FBI and US Secret Service: North Korea's TraderTraitor (North Korea denied involvement))
Summary: FBI and USSS attributed the theft to North Korea's TraderTraitor and urged exchanges and DeFi operators to block transactions with or derived from its addresses; stolen funds were converted mainly to Ethereum. Binance's post-mortem describes a months-long campaign from June 2026: a fake job interview with a malicious coding assignment and "AI coding tool" installer compromised an employee device (~September), the attacker evaded EDR, moved laterally from 20 Oct, reached wallet tooling by 29 Oct and used compromised credentials to authorize transactions. Elliptic traced ~12,000 wallets across 11 blockchains.
Notes: The FBI alert lists wallet addresses; they are not recorded here (not read directly). Theft-date details come from Binance's post-mortem as reported by The Record.
